Antipolo Cathedral is not only a place of worship but also a significant cultural and historical landmark in Rizal. As a graduate of architectute, the cathedral’s architecture is simple yet dignified, featuring a circular dome design that creates a calm and solemn atmosphere inside. Its spacious interior allows large crowds, especially during pilgrimage season, while still maintaining a sense of reverence.

What makes the cathedral truly special is its deep spiritual importance. As the home of Our Lady of Peace and Good Voyage, it has long been a destination for pilgrims, travelers, and devotees seeking guidance and protection. The atmosphere feels peaceful despite the number of visitors, and the surrounding plaza offers a relaxing space for reflection.

Overall, Antipolo Cathedral is a meaningful blend of faith, history, and community. Whether you visit for prayer, pilgrimage, or simply to appreciate its architecture and serene ambiance, it remains one of the most important and cherished religious sites in the Philippines.

I had a generally positive experience at Cloud 9—the store was clean, well-organized, and the staff were friendly and knowledgeable about the products. They took the time to answer my questions and helped me find exactly what I needed without being pushy. The selection was impressive, with a good variety of options at reasonable prices. However, the checkout process felt a bit slow during peak hours, and I noticed that a few popular items were out of stock. Overall, it’s a solid place to shop, and with a little improvement in stock consistency and speed of service, it would easily be a five-star experience.

Food & Service (5/10)
Our dining experience was disappointing. Despite ordering promptly, our meals arrived nearly an hour later—after two newcomers had already finished eating. We had to follow up twice before our food was served, which made the wait frustrating and diminished the overall experience.

View & Ambience
The view of Metro Manila was undeniably beautiful and one of the highlights of the visit. However, the surroundings did not live up to the same standard.

Hanging Bridge: Poorly maintained, with loose metal railings that felt unsafe.

360 Deck: Overcrowded with students lounging around, more focused on chatting than appreciating the view. The area was marred by vandalism, defaced paintings, unsightly padlocks, and scattered trash, making the space feel neglected and uninviting.

Overall Experience
While the panoramic view was worth seeing, the long wait for food, lack of maintenance, and unwelcoming atmosphere overshadowed it. Unfortunately, the visit left us with more frustration than enjoyment, and it wasn’t the great experience we had hoped for.

If you're looking for a spot with fresh air and picturesque views, this is the place to go to, offering a 360° view of both Metro Manila and the surrounding Rizal mountains also fairly accessible via commute.

The entrance fee for the viewing deck alone is a reasonable 100 pesos given you'll first pass the mini museum and hanging bridge. However, if your dining receipt exceeds 300 php (on a per-person basis), you're entitled to a free pass to the 360° deck.

If you're travelling via commute, it is a steep walk up to the common area not including the 360° deck itself. In addition, be wary of overcharging tricycles just near the entrance should your stay extend toward the evening hours. They'll charge you 3x+ the amount you'd pay an air conditioned minibus back to Masinag/Antipolo station.

Overall, a great place to go to offering views and a vantage point as a place to chill, take photos in, etc.

Mystical Cave is perfect for anyone looking for a bit of adventure — with a short trek and an underground cave exploration.

As someone who enjoys a challenge, I tried both! First, there's a 20–30 minute uphill trek (depending on your pace). It’s a bit tiring, but refreshing. At the top, you’ll get to enjoy beautiful mountain views — a nice reward before heading back down.

After that, we started the Mystical Cave tour. The inside of the cave is cool and quiet, and our guide shared interesting stories about its history and natural formation. After about 30–45 minutes, you’ll reach the end of the main path, where you can see beautiful stalagmite formations that almost look like natural crystals — really amazing to see up close.

But if you're up for more adventure, there's a lower section of the cave that's more challenging. The path gets steep, and the man-made ladder there isn’t very sturdy, so be extra careful. It’s also dark, so a flashlight is a must. I made it through, but it wasn’t easy! You’ll need to crawl or slide through tight openings, and even “dive” into narrow parts — it's not for the faint of heart.

Overall, it was a fun and challenging experience — definitely worth it if you’re into nature and adventure.

As you wander from one gallery to another, you’ll find hidden pockets of greenery, cozy seating areas, and terraces overlooking Antipolo’s scenic landscape. Blanco Family of Angono, Rizal is known as the family of Artist. The head of the family, Jose “Pitok” Blanco, influenced his wife and his seven (7) children to create variety of art work that depicts the life in Angono, memories about their travel, and subjects that interest them.

The youngest Blanco, Peter Paul, started his work of art at the age of eleven (11) months. He grew up playing with colors, canvas and brushes at their family studio. He is the youngest artist that exhibited in the Cultural Center of the Philippines and to have a one-man show at the age of nine (9). Peter Paul's subject are his pets and his discoveries around the world.

Gay Blanco is the youngest daughter of Pitok. Contrary to everyone,  Gay learned to draw first before  she could start writing. She was exposed as an Artist during the family exhibit  in Malaysia and Singapore.  In 1983, young Gay won an bronze medal on one of the exhibits that they participated in Hongkong. Gay loves to paint women and children.

Jan Blanco is the fifth child of Pitok. At a young age, Jan showed interest in painting birds. On his paintings he showed how birds are being domesticated and how some freely roam on the fields of Angono. Aside from birds, he is also active in making work of arts related to social concerns such as poverty and ecological balance.

Joy Blanco- Balcita is the eldest daughter of Pitok. Her favorite subject are people of all ages and in different walks of life.

Pitok’s third son Michael started to draw at the age of 10. Among all the members of the family, Michael has the most outstanding portraits. His portraits are detailed, precise and full of life. Aside from portraits, he also excel in landscape and genres particular to the daily activities of his folks.

Noel is the second son of Pitok. He loves all sorts of water form and mood. He consider it as his element and subject.

As the eldest son of Pitok, Glenn was challenged to follow the foot steps and standards of his father. As a young artists he joined local and international exhibits and contest. He loves to paint nature scenery and landscapes. He also mastered the art of drawing and painting tropical fruits, vegetable and flora of rare authenticity.

Loreto Perez Blanco is the loving wife, support and nurturing guidance of the Blanco Family. She loves painting mature woman and mothers that incorporate her feelings and emotions towards raising their family.

Jose Blanco also known as Pitok Blanco is the head of the family. Pitok was born and raised in Angono, Rizal. He graduated in the University of Santo Tomas with the degree in Fine Arts. In 1971, He was able to showcase his work of art on a one-man show. It was also the year that he started to teach and impart his knowledge about art to his family. Pitok’s famous masterpiece is the “Angono Town Fiesta”. It is an oil mural painting that shows the jovial celebration of the San Clemente Festival.

Blanco Family Museum is open daily from 9 AM-12 PM and 1 PM to 5 PM. Admission Fee starts at Php 70.00 for children and senior citizen and Php 100 for adults.

We decided to visit the Angono Petroglyphs, one of those places that quietly reminds you how old this country really is ??????. This site is considered the oldest known work of art in the Philippines, with carvings believed to date back to around 3,000 BC to 1,000 BC, long before written history reached the islands.

It was discovered in 1965 by National Artist Carlos “Botong” Francisco, which alone already gives it serious cultural weight.

To reach the petroglyphs, you enter through a short cave-like tunnel, which honestly adds to the atmosphere. It feels like you’re stepping backward in time, not just walking to an exhibit. Whether you’re visiting solo or with a group, you’ll need to present a valid ID upon entry, which is fair given how fragile and important the site is.

Inside, there’s an information building near the carvings that explains the background and theories behind them. There are about 127 rock carvings, mostly human figures, believed to be linked to rituals, healing, or early spiritual practices. When you actually see them up close, you can’t help but notice how expressive they are. Some clearly look human, while others spark the imagination. I personally saw figures that reminded me of a turtle or a lizard… or maybe it’s just a very well-fed guy etched into stone thousands of years ago ??. That ambiguity is part of the charm. These carvings still make people think, argue, and wonder.

Parking is available near the tunnel entrance, and from there it’s roughly a 5-minute walk to the rock wall itself. The walk is easy and manageable, even if you’re not in hiking shape.
This isn’t a flashy tourist spot, and that’s exactly why it works. It’s quiet, grounded, and deeply Filipino. If you want to understand our roots beyond textbooks and classrooms, this place is absolutely worth the visit. You don’t just see history here. You feel it.

Agono binangonan petroglyphs

The Angono-Binangonan Petroglyphs are a collection of prehistoric rock art carvings located in the town of Angono, Rizal in the Philippines. These petroglyphs are considered the oldest known works of art in the country and are thought to date back to between 3000 and 4000 BCE. They depict various animals, people, and abstract designs and were made by ancient communities living in the area using tools to carve into the rock surface. The petroglyphs are considered an important cultural and historical artifact and are protected as a National Cultural Treasure by the Philippine government.

Baras Church, also known as the Diocesan Shrine and Parish of St. Joseph, was a truly memorable experience. It’s one of the best and most beautiful Catholic churches I’ve ever seen. I was immediately captivated by its rustic stone façade and the peaceful atmosphere that surrounds it. The intricate structure, especially the centuries-old adobe walls and exposed wooden ceiling beams, speaks volumes about the craftsmanship and faith of those who built it.

Baras Church was originally founded in 1595 by Franciscan missionaries and has endured through multiple relocations and reconstructions due to attacks and natural calamities. The current church structure, completed in the 1680s, is considered one of the oldest in Rizal province. Unlike many restored churches, Baras has preserved its original architecture, making the experience feel like a journey back in time.

One fascinating detail is the simplicity of its interiors, which contrasts beautifully with its historical richness. Instead of grand ornamentation, it embraces a more solemn and humble aesthetic that enhances the sacred experience. And if you visit during sundown, the way the light filters through the old windows is breathtaking—it gives the whole place a golden, almost mystical glow.

Whether you’re a history lover, a devout Catholic, or simply someone who appreciates old-world charm, Baras Church is a place worth visiting. It’s not just a site to see, but a space to reflect and feel connected to centuries of faith and tradition.

The Diocesan Shrine and Parish of St. Joseph, also known as Baras Church, is a Roman Catholic church located in Baras, Rizal, Philippines, where the miraculous centuries-old image of San Jose de Baras (Spanish: El Glorioso Patriarca Señor San José de Baras) is enshrined. The church is known to be the oldest parish dedicated to Saint Joseph in the Southern Tagalog Region. The first church was built in 1595 by Franciscan missionaries who established a parish at the town's old site in what is now Boso-Boso in Antipolo, with St. James as its patron.[4] The town and its church was transferred in 1636 to a site called Ibayo to escape the hostilities of the Aeta inhabitants in the area who burned the town and the church in 1635. The second site was located one and one-half leagues (about 7.24 kilometers) southeast of the first site. The church was dedicated to Christ the Savior but it also was affected by hostilities, this time when Chinese rebels in 1639 burned the church as well as other churches in neighboring towns.

The Historical Binangonan Church, or Sta Ursula Parish, has a quiet charm that grows on you the moment you step into its grounds. Founded in 1621 as a Franciscan chapel and later entrusted to the Jesuits in 1679, the place carries four centuries of stories in its walls. The grounds are wide, with generous space for parking, though getting a big vehicle through the entrance can be a bit tricky. Still, once you are inside, the calm setting makes the effort worth it.

Walking into the church feels like stepping into another time. The interior is warm and full of character. The old beams, the soft light around the altar, and the gentle wear on the stone and wood make you slow down without trying. Among the churches in Rizal, Sta Ursula stands out for its beauty. It does not feel staged or modernized. It feels lived in, steady, and honest.

The people around the parish match the place. They greet you with simple kindness, the type that makes visitors feel at home right away. You see locals praying, lighting candles, or sitting quietly. The church is part of their everyday life, and you feel that connection as soon as you enter.

Sta Ursula Parish is not grand, but it leaves a deep and gentle impression.

Santa Ursula Parish Church – Binangonan, Rizal

Also known as Binangonan Church, this place holds a special place in my heart. Coming back here felt nostalgic—like stepping back into childhood memories. I remember how massive the church seemed when I was little. The Jollibee nearby is still there, just like I remembered it, standing as a quiet witness to all those Sunday mornings we spent going to Mass as a family.

The church, named after Saint Ursula, still retains its quiet charm. Its old stone façade, arched doors, and simple but dignified architecture give it an aura of timeless grace. Despite the years, the church looks unbothered—like a place that has stood still while the world around it changed.

Visiting again reminded me not just of the place, but of a rhythm of life that was once so familiar. It was more than just going to church—it was the feeling of being rooted, of childhood Sundays filled with family, prayers, and joy.

Tahimik at solemn yung vibe ng simbahan, bagay talaga sa mga gustong magdasal o mag-reflect. Ang ganda ng architecture classic old-style na may pagka-Baroque, tapos may mga lumang retablo at paintings pa by a local artist, kaya may dating talaga.

Isa rin ‘to sa mga pinakamatandang simbahan sa Rizal, and recently, dineclare na siya as National Cultural Treasure deserve naman kasi ang rich ng history at preserved pa yung details kahit matanda na.

Madaling puntahan since nasa town proper lang siya ng Binangonan. Medyo hassle lang minsan sa parking lalo na pag may misa o event. Pero kung weekday ka pupunta or between masses, mas maaliwalas.

In general, maganda siyang pasyalan pang-picture, pang-pray, at pang-history trip. Di lang siya simbahan, heritage site din.

Sta. Lucia East Grand Mall is a familiar and dependable mall for many people living in Rizal, Marikina, and nearby areas. It may not be the newest mall around, but it continues to serve its purpose well as a place for everyday needs, casual dining, and simple leisure. What makes it appealing is how complete it feels. You can do groceries, shop for essentials, watch a movie, eat with friends, or simply pass time, all in one place.

One of its strongest points is accessibility. With direct access from the LRT Line 2 Marikina Pasig Station and several public transport options nearby, getting to the mall is convenient for commuters. This makes it a common meeting place for students, workers, and families. The mall also offers a wide range of stores, from budget friendly shops to familiar local brands, which makes it practical rather than intimidating.

One of the best things about the mall is its atmosphere. Seasonal decorations are consistently well done and give the space a festive feel throughout the year. The classic fountain at the center remains a recognizable and nostalgic feature, serving as a natural meeting point. Regular marketing events and exhibits add life to the mall, giving visitors something new to see beyond shopping.

While some parts of the mall already show their age, this also gives it a sense of familiarity and character. Overall, Sta. Lucia East Grand Mall remains a relevant, community oriented space that continues to bring people together.

To start off, there are two villas available: Villa 1 and Villa 2. We chose Villa 2, which has three downsides compared to Villa 1: you share the house with the owner (as one reviewer mentioned), there’s no lake view, and it’s smaller. It’s a cheaper option, so if you don’t mind these drawbacks, go for it.
The pool is nice, but the jacuzzi heater didn’t work. Karaoke is allowed only until 10 p.m., which I understand since the owner shares the property, but some guests might see that as a negative. Billiards costs ?100 per hour — it would’ve been nice if that were included, but oh well.
The ambience is chill and cozy. The lights around the pool complement the house party vibe, and the whole place is lined with lights that shine throughout the night.
The lounge and dining areas are great; they can fit the villa’s full capacity. The lounge’s hammock area is nice — I could’ve slept there if I wanted to.
As for the rooms, the interiors are okay: there are small cracks here and there, and the air-con housing is missing and looks broken, but the rooms are cold. They provide thin blankets, so I suggest bringing your own. We even thought at first that some rooms had no bathroom because the bathroom doors blended into the design.
Overall, for the price it could be better. It’s about two hours from Manila, which is convenient, and I hope they fix these issues — I did enjoy my stay despite the problems.

Visiting the Pililla Wind Farm is a refreshing escape just a few hours away from Manila. The sight of the towering windmills lined up along the rolling hills is both breathtaking and calming—parang nasa ibang bansa ang vibes. From the viewing deck, you can enjoy a panoramic view of Laguna de Bay and the surrounding mountains, which makes the place perfect for sightseeing and photography. It’s also a nice spot to unwind because the breeze is cool and relaxing, especially in the late afternoon when the sun sets behind the wind turbines. The area has small stalls selling snacks and souvenirs, making the trip feel more like a laid-back day out. Though it’s not as big as the wind farms in Ilocos, Pililla Wind Farm is very accessible, making it a great quick getaway for families, friends, or even solo travelers who just want to recharge with nature’s view. Definitely worth a stop if you’re exploring Rizal or nearby provinces.

?? Animals & Attractions

??? Navigation
Getting around is manageable thanks to clear signage. Just follow the signs—deviating can be confusing since the area is huge.

You’re allowed to bring your own drinking water and light snacks like biscuits. There are dining areas inside, but food prices are on the higher side. Since it’s located in Montalban, you also have plenty of dining options outside the zoo.

?? Time Needed

Just recently, we dropped by this place on a sunny Saturday afternoon around 3 PM. The folks around were genuinely warm and accommodating, although most of them were stall vendors situated near the entrance of Wawa. If you didn't bring your baon, variety of foods are available, from classic Pares, Shawarma, Fishballs, and Isawan.

Upon arrival, the barkers were courteous enough to guide us to our parking spot. They charge a reasonable fee of 20 pesos per vehicle or motorcycle, covering your entire stay in the park. Even if I didn't bring a bike initially, vendors informed us you could still bring it inside for an additional 20 pesos.

Moving on, we each had to shell out 20 pesos for a one-time entrance fee since it's an eco-park. Upon entering, we had to pass through a tunnel. Wawa awaited us downstairs, but caution was necessary while navigating the rocky terrain. I opted for rubber shoes since swimming wasn't on our agenda; we were merely showing our company visitor around. At the initial section of Wawa, where the falls are located, cottages were conveniently set up for picnics. If you're feeling adventurous, you can venture further. On the opposite side of the falls, you can rent a boat. They offer two options: a 20-minute ride for 400 pesos, where they'll tour you around nearby campsites, or a longer tour lasting up to 45 minutes for 700 pesos, as advised by the boat attendants. We opted for the shorter ride since we weren't dressed for swimming. Nonetheless, it was enjoyable, allowing us to capture picturesque moments in between. By the way, the boats are motorized for easier navigation. However, it's essential to exercise caution as there are no life vests, although the attendants assured us that the water isn't deep. Overall, the attendants were incredibly friendly and accommodating.

During our boat tour, we spotted numerous campsites and rental houses for overnight stays. I'm unsure if they offer Wi-Fi, as the signal wasn't great for both Smart and Globe networks. Cottages were also available along the campsite for those who wished to swim, making it even more convenient. What's even better is that you can bring and cook your own food there, just remember to bring your own utensils and cooking wares. Access to the campsites is only possible via boat rental, making boat rides also serve as transportation. However, if you're daring enough, I noticed other visitors wading through the waters to reach other parts of the campsites.

Overall, it was a pleasant stay with friendly locals in a beautiful setting perfect for family picnics and swimming. I hope their hospitality remains consistent for years to come and continues to improve for the better.

Fact: this cave is used by the Gerilyas during spanish times as a meeting place, and where they plan everything "kung saan sila nag kalinawan ng mga plano". This cave has seven levels but only five is open to the public. Situated in Barangay Tandang Kutyo of Tanay, Rizal, Calinawan Cave is an enormous cave system composed of multiple levels and various chambers and openings. History tells us that the cave served as hideout by Filipino revolutionaries during Spanish-American war, and a shelter during the Second World War. How it got its name, according to local folklore, has a touch of history too, as it was where the Japanese and American troops settle their disputes, thus Calinawan from the Filipino word “linaw” which means to settle or to clear.

But more than its historical significance, the natural beauty of the cave’s interiors and chambers are magnets that attract a lot of people that even films and television productions often use the cave as their shooting location. Sadly, some of them left indelible and irreversible damages to the cave.

Before entering the cave, each person is required to pay Fifty pesos and Two hundred pesos for the Guide. Every visitor must wear safety helmets because of the risk hidden inside the cave. You will experience many challenges while inside the cave.  For teens and young adults, I will definitely advice that you wear Dark colored clothes because you will have to crawl on a narrow part. Unless you are "maarte" then you can use the senior citizen's way.

More great adventures are hidden inside this cave. It is told that Calinawan cave has othe entrance but it was bombed by the Japanese soldiers during world war two since they used the cave as a hospital and a hideout. And for you to travel end to end, you will spend 9 days and 9 nights inside the cave.  But unluckily, those levels are closed. So the guides will only bring you to the maximum of fifth level only. Which you will last for approximately 45 minutes to 1 hour inside the cave if you want to finish all the five levels.

I visited Regina RICA a few weeks ago, and it was a peaceful and spiritually uplifting experience. Parking is accessible, and the site is well-organized for pilgrims and visitors alike. This place is more than just a tourist spot—it’s a pilgrimage site and sacred sanctuary nestled in the mountains of Tanay.

To reach the iconic 71-foot-tall statue of Our Lady of the Holy Rosary (Regina Rosarii), you’ll need to take a short walk uphill. The path is both calming and reflective, allowing time to prepare your mind and spirit. Along the way, you’ll notice footprints embedded in the pavement—each marked with a name. These likely belong to generous donors or pilgrims who have contributed to the sanctuary’s development, adding a deeply personal and communal touch to the journey.

Once you reach the statue—affectionately called “Mama Mary on the Hill”—you’ll discover that it has an interior chapel. Please note that modest clothing is required; mini skirts, see-through attire, and sleeveless tops aren’t allowed as a sign of reverence. Visitors are also reminded to keep silent inside the statue, as it’s a place for meditation and prayer. I saw two nuns seated quietly in contemplation, which added to the serene and sacred atmosphere.

Inside the statue is a small altar. Being there felt calming and intimate. When you step out from the top area of the statue, you’re greeted with a breathtaking view of the surrounding Sierra Madre mountains—a moment that feels both humbling and beautiful.

I also visited the modern chapel within the grounds. Though its design is contemporary, it still feels deeply sacred. The peaceful atmosphere, combined with the natural surroundings, enhances the prayerful experience.

Regina RICA was established by the Dominican Sisters of Regina Rosarii and has become a popular destination for pilgrims and nature lovers. It offers a unique blend of faith, silence, nature, and healing, making it an ideal place to pause, reflect, and reconnect—whether you’re Catholic or simply seeking quiet time.

Regina Rica is a popular pilgrimage site located in Tanay, Rizal, Philippines. It features a 71-foot statue of the Our Lady of Regina Rica, which translates to "Queen of the Rich Harvest." The site offers stunning views of the Sierra Madre mountains and the Laguna de Bay.
Features and Activities
1. Statue and Shrine: The massive statue of Our Lady of Regina Rica is the centerpiece, surrounded by a peaceful and serene environment.
2. Garden and Walkway: Visitors can stroll through the beautifully landscaped gardens and walkways, perfect for reflection and meditation.
3. *Chapel and Prayer Areas*: The site has designated areas for prayer, confession, and worship.
4. *Retreat and Recollection*: Regina Rica offers facilities for retreats, recollections, and team-building activities.
5. *Hiking and Outdoor Activities*: The surrounding mountains and forests provide opportunities for hiking, trekking, and nature exploration.

Visitor Information
1. *Location*: Sitio Aguho, Barangay Sampaloc, Tanay, Rizal
2. *Operating Hours*: 8:00 AM - 5:00 PM (subject to change)
3. *Dress Code*: Modest attire recommended
4. *Food and Beverages*: Available at the site's cafeteria and food stalls

# Getting There
1. *By Private Vehicle*: From Manila, take Marcos Highway, then turn left at the Tanay Municipal Hall.
2. *By Public Transportation*: Take a jeepney or van from Shaw Boulevard or Cubao to Tanay, then hire a tricycle to Regina Rica.

Step into history at Tanay Church — Rizal’s 300-Year-Old Baroque Masterpiece!

On our recent Tanay Familiarization Tour, we uncovered the timeless beauty of San Ildefonso de Toledo Parish Church, famously known as Tanay Church. Built by Franciscan friars in the late 1700s, this stunning stone and wood structure is the best-preserved colonial church in Rizal province.

Finished in 1783, its grand Baroque façade features delicate arches, intricate angelic sculptures, and classic pilasters that tell tales of faith and Filipino artistry. Inside, five ornate altarpieces and a magnificent pulpit showcase the rich craftsmanship of Filipino artisans through the centuries.

Declared a National Cultural Treasure by the National Museum of the Philippines in 2001, Tanay Church is more than just a historic site—it’s a living legacy of culture, devotion, and architectural brilliance.

Visiting here isn’t just sightseeing; it’s stepping back into centuries of Filipino heritage. History lovers, architecture buffs, and spiritual seekers — this church is a must-visit!

5 Fascinating Facts About Tanay Church:
??Built in 1783: The church has stood for over 300 years, surviving earthquakes and wars.
??Franciscan Roots: It was constructed by Franciscan friars using local stone and hardwood.
??Baroque Beauty: The façade is rich with Baroque details like angel sculptures, arches, and pilasters.
??National Cultural Treasure: Officially declared by the National Museum in 2001 for its historical and cultural significance.
??Five Altarpieces Inside: Each altar is intricately designed, showcasing exquisite local craftsmanship.

San Ildefonso de Toledo Parish Church – Tanay, Rizal (Diocese of Antipolo)

One of the best churches in both exterior and interior. Although the exteriors have undergone some reconstruction, the interior has remained beautifully intact throughout history. The sculpture in the altar is stunning—rich in detail and devotion. The Stations of the Cross along the walls are particularly eye-catching, with intricate carvings that feel alive with emotion and story.

You’ll also notice a number of religious paintings throughout the church, adding depth and color to the sacred atmosphere. When you go near the altar, look up and you’ll be greeted by the beautiful fresco-style ceiling art—especially the octagonal dome surrounded by painted medallions of saints and biblical figures.

A charming and unexpected touch? Look closely at those ceiling medallion paintings—yes, those are actual bats quietly hanging there! They’re not part of the artwork but real, tiny residents of the church. It’s an amusing and oddly heartwarming reminder that this is a living, breathing piece of history—still connected to nature and time, even as it preserves centuries of devotion.

Parking Insight: Easily accessible for both cars and motorcycles, even on Sundays.

Amazing that this oldest of Tanay churches is still standing! But before entering the church, the huge sculpture of Mama Mary and San Ildefonso of Toledo greets parishioners as they enter the gate. The sculpture was made by several local craftsmen as a way to preserve the giant 100-year old acacia tree that was dying of disease.
This sculpture is echoed by at least 14 other ones inside the church that represent the stations of the cross - one of the most beautiful depictions of major events in the Bible. These are encased in glass and should live a long long time for future generations to marvel at.
The church looks its age although I think it has been remodeled or restored several times. It's in baroque style and has a beautiful retablo. Some of the stonework might still be original, or at least very very old. There are also wonderful sculptures of saints mounted on walls, as well as a richly adorned santo entierro.
The side pulpit has a life-sized figure of a smiling Pope Francis looking over the entire church (probably made out of corrugated paper or very thin wood) - a nice reminder of the Pope's last visit to the Philippines.
A large courtyard opens out at the side of the church, with the statue of Mama Mary dominating the square. Other wonderful details of the church must be experienced to be fully admired.

Very beautiful nature park ! We had a great time and made some new friends with fellow park goers. As we went on a Weds, the park was not crowded at all. Some things to note when visiting:

1. We paid at 3 diff points for our hike along the river, totaling p165/pax. This is outside guide/environmental fees paid at the start etc.

2. To go from Manila, take a UV van from starmall to Tanay (p100/head) and then a trike up to the jump off point (p250/head) ??. Follow the same way back. Start early at 4/5am

3. Wear covered shoes!!! Trail is extremely slippery at parts especially after rain. Shoes might get soaked in the river but any other footwear will make it hard to climb rocks/steep terrain.

4. There is an option to go tubing for 45 mins down the river for p400/head. It’s a bit ex but do this if you can!! It’s a great way to see and experience the river.

5. Some trikes will try to convince you to ride from the river to the jump off point. It is actually a very walkable distance so you can avoid this ride and save some money if you wish. You might hav to ask a local for directions along the way but they are usually more than willing to help.

6. If you are in a group of 2 or less, consider joining another group to save cost on the tour guide fee (p500). One tour guide can take up to 5 people.

Limestone rock formations are primarily composed of calcium carbonate in the form of a mineral called calcite. These rocks were formed underwater from secretions of marine life forms millions of years ago and uplifted due to tectonic processes. It is extensively distributed throughout the Philippines since the climate and environment highly favors its development.

The limestone formations outcrop along Tinipak River and its vicinity are characterized by geomorphological feature called Karst Topography. Such features are caused by the dissolution of carbonaceous rocks when in contact with acidic rainwater which forms caves, caverns and other dissolution features.

A beautiful and culturally significant church in Rizal. It was originally built by Franciscan missionaries and later administered by the Jesuits. Today, it stands as a grand stone church, with ample parking spaces serving the growing community of Taytay parishioners.

Interestingly, Saint Pedro Calungsod was once assigned here as an altar boy centuries ago.

Recognized for its historical and spiritual importance, it was granted the status of a minor basilica and the first in the province.

The parish itself dates to the 16th century, but this church has been completely rebuilt over the centuries. Nevertheless, it is still significant enough to have been named a minor Basilica in 2024, one of only 23 in the Philippines. My family has ties to this parish going back many years so we enjoy visiting.

Taytay Church, now officially declared as a Minor Basilica, is one of the biggest and most awe-inspiring churches I’ve ever visited. The moment we arrived, I was captivated by its majestic façade and the attention to detail that went into its design—both inside and out. You can truly feel the deep devotion and heritage preserved in its walls.

The church was originally founded in 1579 by the Jesuits, making it one of the oldest parishes in the Philippines. It was later taken over by the Franciscans and then the secular clergy. Over the centuries, Taytay Church has withstood natural disasters and undergone several reconstructions—each time preserving its historical character while continuing to serve as a center of faith.

Fun fact: The bell tower and the main structure you see today date back to the 1800s, and some of the stones used in construction are said to have come from the ruins of Fort Santiago. Its elevation to a Minor Basilica in 2024 is a rare and honorable recognition, highlighting its spiritual and cultural significance not only to Taytay but to the whole of Rizal province.

Since we visited on a Sunday, the church was understandably crowded, and parking was a bit difficult. We parked outside, which seems to be the norm on weekends. I imagine it’s a lot more peaceful on weekdays, allowing more time to reflect and appreciate the space. I really wanted to explore the interior and exterior more thoroughly, but it felt a bit awkward to roam around during Mass—haha!

Nonetheless, the entire experience was memorable. The community’s warmth, the church’s beauty, and its long-standing history make Taytay Church a must-visit for anyone interested in architecture, history, or faith. You don’t just visit Taytay Church—you witness a living legacy.

Taytay Sports Complex is a welcome public space that gives the community room to move, train, and breathe. It stands out mainly as a place for everyday fitness rather than a flashy sports venue. The oval track and open field are the main highlights, offering runners, walkers, and athletes a proper area to exercise without worrying about traffic or tight streets. The space feels open and functional, which is exactly what a town sports complex should be.

One of its strongest points is accessibility. The complex is free to use and open to the public, making it friendly to students, families, and casual fitness enthusiasts. Early mornings are especially lively, with joggers and walkers sharing the track in a calm and orderly way. The atmosphere encourages discipline and community, not competition.

That said, the complex is still a work in progress. Some facilities are limited, and visitors can feel that development is ongoing. Parking can be a challenge at busy hours, and the fixed closing time limits use for people who prefer evening workouts. Despite these limits, the place serves its purpose well.

Overall, Taytay Sports Complex is a valuable investment for public health and community life. It may not be complete yet, but it already plays an important role in encouraging active and healthy habits.

We stayed for one night, and here are our key takeaways:

Pros:

Excellent Staff: Super friendly, responsive, and available even late at night. Their hospitality was the best part of our stay.

Beautiful Cabins: The cabins were well-designed and the surrounding plants and flower beds added a nice, aesthetic touch. It attracts birds and bees as well. That was cool!

Comfortable Basics: Air conditioning worked well, and the bathroom water pressure was just right. The kitchen was huge.

Cons:

Dirty Pool: The water seemed poorly maintained—not dirty with debris, but the water itself smelled bad and left stains. I couldn’t let my 1.5-year-old swim.

Bathroom Issues: No toilet seat, no countertop, and the faucet looked patched together. The space didn’t match the vibe of the listing.

Worn Play Area: The play structure and hammock were rough and dusty. Not at all what the listing was trying to convey.

Missing Amenities: “Pack and play” was listed but not available. The host wasn’t even aware it was offered. Karaoke was grounded. They needed to turn of the filter at the pool to solve the issue.

Not a negative thing perse. There were a few dogs and cats that roam around the space, Just be careful of your food and make sure to keep them away/covered. They are mostly friendly. The FLIES though were overwhelming despite food covers—fly traps would have helped.

Strong Odors: Farm smells are expected, but the mix of cow dung and stagnant water was unusually intense.

We availed of the night package for this location.

First, the travel was so unbelievably far. No kidding. You're gonna have to travel through a long trail from the main road in order to get to somewhere around the area and once you're there, there's a hidden trail that's like a 10min walk to the place itself. Basically in terms of travel, get ready to encounter a lot of road and bumpy terrain. I highly suggest using a big car for transportation.

Secondly, the place itself. Do manage your expectations because it will give you a provincial feel. Some people appreciate this, some don't so it's important to keep that in mind. There are dogs present that will hover you during mealtime and there are so much flies during the day. Like, SO MUCH flies. It was a bit concerning, to be quite honest haha
At night, it gave off a comfy feel. During sunrise, it was so peaceful because of its seclusion but it is close to a farm, so there's a certain odor that you may or may not tolerate.
The rooms are spacious and a bit cozy especially at night, but at daytime the AC is a challenge because it's too hot around the area, so it's a bit hard to feel cool even in the comfort of your rooms.

The owners are definitely accommodating about all requests are so easy to talk with and their caretaker, Ate Leah, is really nice and will assist you as much as she can.

Overall, it was an okay or average experience.
